before.title: 1.2 PureTech Wet Timing Belt Degradation / Failure (Mokka B)
before.description: The second-generation Mokka B (built on the Stellantis CMP platform) uses the PSA/Stellantis 1.2 PureTech (EB2) three-cylinder turbo with a 'wet' timing belt that runs submerged in engine oil. Fuel dilution and oil contamination cause the belt rubber to break down prematurely; shed particles clog the oil pump pick-up strainer, starving the engine of oil, and the belt itself can skip teeth or snap. Because it is an interference engine, belt failure typically destroys valves and pistons. Affected cars also show excessive oil consumption. Stellantis acknowledged the defect and runs a PureTech compensation platform covering documented oil-consumption and premature-belt expenses on 1.0/1.2 PureTech cars, with extended warranty up to 10 years / 112,000 miles under conditions.
before.solution: Strictly follow the (shortened) oil-and-belt service interval with the correct low-SAPS oil; replace the wet belt, tensioner and oil pump strainer preventively (many indies convert/replace early). If oil consumption or belt debris is found, submit a claim through the Stellantis PureTech compensation portal / authorised dealer; catastrophic failures require a full engine rebuild or replacement.
symptoms: Loss of power or sudden engine failure

citations.title: Stellantis opens wet belt compensation portal for UK customers - Fleet News

before.title: 1.4 Turbo Timing Chain Stretch / Cold-Start Rattle (A14NET/B14NET)
before.description: The 1.4 Turbo petrol (GM Family-0, A14NET/B14NET) fitted to the first-gen Mokka and Mokka X suffers from timing-chain stretch and tensioner/guide wear, often appearing from around 80,000-100,000 km. A stretched chain alters valve timing and, if it skips, can cause serious internal engine damage. The classic symptom is a metallic rattle for a few seconds on cold start. Owners on the Mokka Owners Club report needing chain, tensioner and sometimes turbo/water-pump work, with cars off the road for extended periods. Cars used mostly for short trips and frequent stop-start cycles tend to wear faster.
before.solution: Diagnose chain stretch via crank/cam correlation and cam-timing fault codes; replace the timing chain, tensioner, guides and sprockets as a kit, using genuine/quality parts and the correct oil and service intervals to prevent recurrence. Address any related turbo or water-pump wear at the same time while the front is apart.

before.title: 1.6 CDTI EGR Valve & Cooler Carbon Clogging (P0401)
before.description: The 1.6 CDTI diesel (B16DTH/B16DTU, 'Whisper Diesel') in the Mokka X is prone to heavy carbon build-up in the EGR valve, EGR cooler and intake, especially on city-driven cars. The ECU infers EGR flow from the MAF signal, so any restriction triggers P0401 (insufficient EGR flow) and rough running or limp mode. A separate failure is the vacuum-operated EGR-cooler bypass-flap actuator, whose spindle can snap. Forum reports (Mokka Owners Club) document recurring P0401, often combined with MAF/MAP faults.
before.solution: Remove and ultrasonically clean the EGR valve, throttle body and intake pipe; in many cases the EGR cooler is fully clogged or the bypass flap is broken and must be replaced. Verify MAF/MAP sensors and vacuum lines. Regular motorway runs and good-quality diesel reduce recurrence.

before.title: Air Conditioning Condenser Leak / Compressor Failure
before.description: The Mokka/Mokka X air-conditioning system frequently loses cooling performance at relatively low mileage. Common root causes are a leaking condenser (mounted low at the front and vulnerable to stone damage and corrosion), a defective expansion valve, or a failing compressor; 2018-build cars are noted as particularly affected. Owners report the system going empty repeatedly after being regassed, indicating an active refrigerant leak.
before.solution: Leak-test the system (UV dye / electronic sniffer / nitrogen pressure test) to locate the leak; replace the condenser, expansion valve or compressor as required, evacuate and recharge with the correct refrigerant and oil. Replacing the receiver/drier is recommended when the system is opened.

before.title: Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF) Clogging & Failed Regeneration
before.description: On the CDTI diesel Mokka/Mokka X driven mainly on short city journeys, the DPF cannot reach the temperature needed for passive/active regeneration and progressively clogs with soot, often as early as 30,000-50,000 km. This produces reduced power, increased fuel use, repeated regeneration warnings and exhaust aftertreatment fault codes; a blocked DPF that never completes regeneration eventually needs forced regen or replacement. The issue is tightly linked to the EGR carbon problem on the same engines.
before.solution: Take the car on regular sustained motorway drives to allow active regeneration; when clogged, perform a forced (static) regeneration with a diagnostic tool or professional DPF clean. A failed/blocked filter must be replaced. Fix any underlying EGR, injector or sensor faults that prevent successful regen.

before.title: Dual-Mass Flywheel Rattle / Clutch Judder (Manual Diesel)
before.description: First-gen Mokka and Mokka X manual diesels (1.6/1.7 CDTI) commonly develop a metallic rattling or ringing noise from the bellhousing area, most noticeable at idle when warm or on the over-run. The cause is wear of the dual-mass flywheel's internal damper springs, sometimes accompanied by clutch judder on take-up. In advanced cases the pedal can stick and start-up becomes noisy. It is frequently misdiagnosed as an engine noise.
before.solution: Confirm DMF wear (excess rotational free-play, characteristic rattle) and replace the dual-mass flywheel; because the gearbox must come out, the clutch kit (and often the slave cylinder) is replaced at the same time to avoid duplicate labour.
symptoms: Metallic rattle/ringing from bellhousing at idle

before.title: Mokka-e 12V Auxiliary Battery Drain
before.description: Mokka-e (and closely related Corsa-e, Peugeot e-208, DS 3 Crossback E-Tense — all CMP/eCMP platform) drains the 12V AGM auxiliary battery during long parking spells, leaving the car unable to wake or charge. Owners report drain as fast as 3-5 days of inactivity. The MyOpel smartphone app polling the car wakes systems and accelerates drain. Stellantis acknowledged the issue and pushed multiple software updates between 2021-2024 — Opel recalled ~13,507 Corsa/Combo/Mokka in Germany alone for the traction battery control software.
before.solution: Update vehicle software to latest (dealer can check; some VINs covered by recall). Use a 12V battery maintainer for parked stretches over 1 week. Disable MyOpel remote polling if parking long-term. AGM 12V replacement needs coding — DIY is risky; dealer cost ~€290 (€150-€250 battery + €50-€100 fit/code).

before.title: Mokka-e Onboard AC Charger (Mahle 11kW) Failure
before.description: The electric Mokka-e (and Corsa-e platform sibling) suffers from failures of the Mahle 11 kW three-phase onboard charger (OBC). before.title: Start-Stop System Malfunction / 12V Battery Parasitic Drain (ICE)
before.description: Combustion-engine Mokka/Mokka X owners frequently report the Start-Stop system ceasing to function alongside a flat or weak 12V battery, sometimes after the car stands for a week or two. The AGM/EFB battery and its state-of-charge management are central: when voltage dips below roughly 11.6V the ECU disables Start-Stop and can lose learned parameters. Some cases are simple battery wear or a marginal alternator, but persistent parasitic drains (modules not sleeping) have left some cars repeatedly going flat even after battery replacement.
before.solution: Test the battery and alternator first and fit the correct AGM/EFB battery with proper coding/registration; if drain persists, perform a parasitic-draw test to find the module/circuit staying awake and repair it. Ensure software is up to date.
symptoms: Repeated battery replacement without fixing drain
